Agent [[Pipelines]]
in Java
scenes.subtitle: Chain agents with typed outputs and gates

lines.say: In episode one, two agents worked together. But they passed plain text, and the second agent always ran.
Today, you'll turn them into a real pipeline: typed data between agents, and a check in plain Java that can stop early.
It's the most common multi-agent pattern, and the easiest to get right.

scenes.heading: What is an agent [[pipeline]]?
items: Agents run in a **fixed order**, like an assembly line
Each agent's **output is the next agent's input**
**Gates** between steps: plain Java checks that can stop the line

lines.say: So, what is an agent pipeline?
Agents run in a fixed order, like an assembly line.
Each agent's output becomes the next agent's input.
Every step has one small job, so every step is easier to get right.
And between steps, you can add gates: plain Java checks that decide if the line continues.

scenes.heading: Pass [[typed data]], not text

rows.label: Free text
rows.text: Hard to check in code: you'd have to parse sentences

rows.label: Structured outputs
rows.text: Claude's answer must follow a JSON schema

rows.label: Java records
rows.text: The SDK builds the schema from your record, and parses the answer

scenes.banner: Check the data in Java, not with another LLM call

lines.say: The key idea is typed data.
If an agent answers in free text, your code can't easily check it. You'd have to parse sentences.
With structured outputs, Claude's answer must follow a JSON schema you give it.
And in Java, you don't even write the schema. The SDK builds it from a record, and parses the answer back into that record.
lines.tts: And in Java, you don't even write the schema. The S D K builds it from a record, and parses the answer back into that record.

lines.say: So you can check the data with normal Java code. No extra LLM call.

left.title: Use a pipeline when…
left.body:
• The steps are known

• You can check the

right.title: Use something else when…
right.body:
• The next step depends
  on what you find
  (routing: next episode)
• One prompt already
  does the job well

lines.say: When should you use a pipeline?
When the steps are known in advance, always in the same order, and you can check each result.
If the next step depends on what you find, that's routing. That's the next episode. And if one prompt already works, keep it simple.

left.title: Episode 1
left.body:
Reviewer → free text notes

Writer always runs,
even with nothing to fix

No way to check

right.body:
Reviewer → a Review record
(line, severity, problem, fix)

✓ Writer only runs

lines.say: We'll upgrade the code-review team from episode one.
Before: the Reviewer wrote free text notes, and the Writer always ran, even when there was nothing to fix.
After: the Reviewer returns a Review record. A gate in Java drops the low-severity bugs, and stops if nothing serious is left. The Writer only runs when it's needed.
Here's the team from episode one.

do.text:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 http://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <groupId>agent</groupId>
    <artifactId>java-agent-pipeline</artifactId>
    <version>1.0</version>

    <properties>
        <maven.compiler.release>17</maven.compiler.release>
        <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
        <!-- The class to run (change it with -Dexec.mainClass=...) -->
        <exec.mainClass>agent.ReviewPipeline</exec.mainClass>
    </properties>

    <dependencies>
        <!-- The official Anthropic Java SDK -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>com.anthropic</groupId>
            <artifactId>anthropic-java</artifactId>
            <version>3.3.0</version>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

    <build>
        <plugins>
            <!-- Lets us run the pipeline with: mvn compile exec:java -->
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.codehaus.mojo</groupId>
                <artifactId>exec-maven-plugin</artifactId>
                <version>3.5.0</version>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>

lines.say: The Reviewer returns a string. My code can't tell if it found zero bugs or ten.
So the Writer always runs, and always costs tokens.

do.match: String report = writer.run("Write the report:\n" + notes);
do.label: Always runs

lines.say: Step one: typed answers. I create Review dot java.
lines.tts: Step one: typed answers. I create Review dot java.

lines.say: A review has a short summary, and a list of bugs.
Each bug has a line number, a severity, the problem, and the fix.

do.match: public record Bug(int line, Severity severity,
do.label: One bug

lines.say: Severity is an enum: low, medium or high. Claude can only answer with one of these three values.

do.match: public enum Severity { LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH }
do.label: Only 3 values

lines.say: That's the contract between the two agents. Plain Java records.
Step two: upgrade the Agent class. The top is the same as in episode one.
Now the new part: a run method with a type. You give it a class, and you get an object of that class back.
One line does the magic: output config with the type. The SDK turns the record into a JSON schema, and Claude's answer must match it.
lines.tts: One line does the magic: output config, with the type. The S D K turns the record into a JSON schema, and Claude's answer must match it.

lines.say: The loop is the same as before. Structured outputs work together with tools in the same request.
When Claude is done, I don't return text anymore. I return the typed object, already parsed.
And the old run method still works. It asks for a small Answer record, and returns its text. So text agents, like our Writer, don't change.
Step three: the gate. In ReviewPipeline dot java.
lines.tts: Step three: the gate. In ReviewPipeline dot java.

lines.say: The gate is plain Java. No LLM, no tokens.
It keeps only the bugs that are not low severity. Because the review is typed, it's one simple filter.
And because it's a normal method, I can unit test it without calling the API.
Step four: build the pipeline. The two agents are the same as in episode one.
Step one of the pipeline: the Reviewer returns a Review object, not a string.
Here I pass Review dot class. That's the only change for a typed agent.
lines.tts: Here I pass Review dot class. That's the only change for a typed agent.

lines.say: Then the gate. If no serious bugs are left, the pipeline stops here. The Writer is never called.
Otherwise, the Writer gets only the serious bugs. Less input, cleaner context.

do.label: Only serious bugs

cards.title: Type every handoff
cards.text: A record between agents, not free text

cards.title: Gate in plain Java
cards.text: Free, fast, and easy to test

cards.title: Pass only what's needed
cards.text: Serious bugs only, not the whole review

cards.title: Test steps offline
cards.text: Fake inputs, no API key needed

lines.say: Four tips for your pipelines.
One: type every handoff. A record between agents, not free text.
Two: write your gates in plain Java. They're free, fast, and easy to test.
Three: pass only what the next agent needs. Our Writer gets the serious bugs, not the whole review.
And four: test each step offline, with fake inputs.

scenes.heading: Recap
items: A pipeline = agents in a **fixed order**, one job each
[[Gates]] in plain Java stop early and save tokens

lines.say: Let's recap.
A pipeline is agents in a fixed order, each with one job.
Pass typed data between them: a Java record, and output config with its type.
And gates in plain Java check each step, stop early, and save tokens.
